paragraphs.source_en: Using various sources of information the chronology of the Round Head paintings may be assessed. Whereas the two most frequently represented animals, mouflon and antelope, are able to live in both dry and wet climates, the water-dependent large wild fauna could only be present in the region under a wet climate. Such favourable climatic and environmental conditions occurred in the Central Sahara in the 11th and 10th millennium BP, and lasted roughly until the 6th millennium BP.

paragraphs.source_en: Important changes took place in the Early Holocene not only in the environment when vegetation and extended water bodies formed in the Central Sahara but also in the cultural and economic sphere of huntergatherers. Human occupation in the Central Saharan massifs is certainly documented in the 10th millennium BP in the Epipalaeolithic period showing new elements such as microlithic industry, grinding stones and pottery production. These populations were particularly interested in mouflon as a hunting prey and similar interest also appears in the Round Head paintings, dominated by images of mouflon and antelope.

paragraphs.source_en: The pottery, dated to the 10th millennium BP, represents a new technology suggesting a new subsistence strategy based on vegetal food, supporting by grinding stones which appeared in the same period. However, the carefully incised decoration of a limited range of motifs, often similar to the body decoration motifs of Round Head anthropomorphic figures, tells a lot about the aesthetic feeling perceptible in both paintings and in the pottery. Pottery decoration is an indicator of an artistic tradition which would not remain limited to the pottery but it would also find its expression in the rock paintings, showing some similarities not only in the motifs but also in the homogeneity and in the conservatism of forms.

paragraphs.source_en: The set of presented arguments from the archaeological and climatological record and from the paintings strongly favour the high chronology of the Round Heads. Such a conclusion is not surprising in an area surrounded by rock art and other artistic evidence in neighbouring regions which are much older than the 10th millennium BP. The Round Head paintings belong to the ancient African artistic tradition and they may have originated in the Early Holocene during a period of substantial change in the climate and environment, causing a new way of life and probably a new way of thinking. This change would be visible in the rock art, in the evolution of forms from simple towards more elaborate ones, and it was related to new territories being explored for the image-making.
